title: A Thousand Heads
hookLine: a person with a thousand heads who is all this and still more: the Veda's first picture of god in everything
carry: god is in all this, every face included
tomorrow: if god is everything, is everything all of god?

cards: A festival crowd, photographed from a rooftop. At first it looks like one moving surface. Then you zoom in.
Heads, thousands of them. Hands in the air. Sandals, a child on someone's shoulders.
One crowd, and countless people, and you can't quite say where one ends and the next begins.

The Rig Veda has a hymn that opens on a picture like that, except the crowd is one person, and the person is bigger than the world. After a hymn that asked who knows, here's one that begins by describing.

teach.b: Purusha means person. Here, in the Rig Veda, it names a cosmic person, and the hymn opens: sahasra-shirsha purushah.

teach.h: A THOUSAND HEADS, EYES AND FEET.
teach.b: The Purusha has a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, a thousand feet. Many readers hear thousand as beyond counting: every head is in some sense his, every pair of eyes, every step.
He covered the earth on every side, and stood beyond it by ten fingers' width. Not a mountain more: ten fingers.

teach.h: PURUSHA EVA IDAM SARVAM: ALL THIS.
teach.b: Then verse two: purusha eva idam sarvam. The Purusha is all this, whatever has been and whatever is to be.
This is one of the oldest seeds of a teaching Hindus carry everywhere: the divine isn't somewhere else, behind the sky. It's here, in all this.
The Upanishads say it again later, sarvam khalv idam brahma, all this is Brahman.

teach.h: NAMASTE: BOWING TO THE DIVINE IN YOU.
teach.b: And many Hindus explain their everyday greeting the same way: the folded hands of namaste bow to the divine in the person in front of you. So that rooftop crowd isn't a mass of strangers.
On the hymn's picture, every face in it is one of the thousand.
Next time you're squeezed into a crowded train or a packed school hallway, that's the Purusha Sukta's view: one sacred person, looking out through all those eyes. And still, ten fingers more.

how: The Purusha Sukta is recited in Hindu worship and Vedic chanting; its 'the Purusha is all this' is one root of the Hindu teaching that the divine is present in everything, which many Hindus connect with namaste.

a hymn to the first king who ruled the earth

games.why: purusha eva idam sarvam: the Purusha is all this. it's one root of the Hindu teaching that the divine is in everything, every face included.

practice: Bring to mind three faces you'll see today: someone you love, someone you pass without noticing, someone who's hard for you. Fold your hands at your chest, and for each one, bow a little, inwardly, the way namaste does.
If you pray, see the divine looking out through their eyes; if you don't, simply wish each of them well.

wordCard.voice: The Purusha Sukta. The hymn of the cosmic person: a thousand heads, eyes and feet, all that has been and will be, and still ten fingers more.

orig.note: Sanskrit: a person, a human being. In Rig Veda 10.90 it names the cosmic person.

carryVoice: Your line: God is in all this, every face included. A thousand heads, and still ten fingers more. See you tomorrow.
